query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating ultrathin, well‐bonded graphene interfacial layers into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy will arrest crack initiation and propagation, thereby significantly improving its mechanical integrity (e.g., higher strength and ductility) without degrading its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy known for its strong caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field conditions but that suffers from poor structural integrity and a tendency to crack under load.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled amount of monolayer or few-layer graphene (via in-situ transfer, deposition, or mixing methods) so that the alloy develops a nanolayered architecture in which graphene is preferentially located at grain boundaries or interfacial regions.
generation.conditions: Test under operational conditions where the caloric effect is active (e.g., room temperature to moderate temperatures and under cycling magnetic/pressure fields) and subject the samples to standard mechanical loading (compression/tensile tests at typical strain rates).
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale graphene layers acting as crack arresters and interfacial reinforcements, which effectively blunt crack tips and impede adverse dislocation motions.
generation.mechanism: Graphene’s exceptional toughness and high tensile strength, along with its ability to form strong interfacial bonds, will serve to delay or arrest the propagation of microcracks. This modification is expected to enhance mechanical properties (increased yield/compressive strength and ductility) without interfering significantly with the crystallographic phase transitions that underpin the caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the graphene-integrated composite will exhibit a directional increase in fracture toughness and mechanical strength (e.g., >20% improvement) while retaining its high caloric performance (with less than ~10% reduction in performance metrics) under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
generation.baseline: The pristine (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy that displays large caloric effects but suffers from mechanical cracking and poor integrity.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold as long as the graphene layers are uniformly distributed and remain chemically inert with respect to the alloy’s active transformation phases. However, if the processing leads to agglomerated or poorly bonded graphene, or if the interfaces disturb the phase transition kinetics critical to the caloric response (e.g., under extreme field intensities or temperatures far outside the tested range), the benefits might not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the crack-arresting concept demonstrated in nanolayered CoCrFeNi/graphene composites (e.g., PMC9227879 evidence) and the strengthening seen in ceramic-reinforced HEA matrix composites (e.g., PMC10222374 evidence). What is new here is the application of a graphene interfacial strategy specifically in a caloric-function high-entropy alloy to overcome cracking without sacrificing its functional performance. Uncertainty remains regarding the detailed influence of the graphene interfaces on the phase transformation kinetics that drive the caloric response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and (2) the same alloy modified by incorporating ultrathin graphene layers, ensuring a uniform nanolayered structure. Conduct identical mechanical tests (compressive and tensile strength, fracture toughness) and caloric performance measurements (e.g., calorimetry and field cycling tests) under the same temperature and field conditions.
measurements: Fracture toughness/damage tolerance (e.g., using crack propagation analysis)
Caloric effect metrics (e.g., entropy change or refrigerant capacity under applied fields)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 15-20% enhancement in mechanical integrity) while maintaining its caloric response within a 10% variation compared to the pristine alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 16 shows the compressive engineering stress–strain curves of the CrFeCuMnNi-x vol.% Al2O3 HEAMCs. The ultimate compressive strength (UCS) and the corresponding compressive strain at the ultimate point are shown in Figure 17. The results of Figure 16 and Figure 17 demonstrate that the compressive strength of the developed HEAMCs increased steadily with the increase in Al2O3 in the CrFeCuMnNi matrix. However, the corresponding strain at the ultimate point decreased, indicating a decrease in plasticity. The microstructure development after hot foring decreased the grain size of the CrFeCuMnNi matrix (Figure 10, Figure 11 and Figure 12). In general, grain refinement can enhance the strength and suppress ductility, owing to the formation of more grain boundaries (producing more surface defects) and leading to a diminished dislocation motion []. The UCS values of 872, 954, 1025, and 1058 MPa were obtained for the CrFeCuMnNi, CrFeCuMnNi-1 vol.% Al2O3, CrFeCuMnNi-2 vol.% Al2O3, and CrFeCuMnNi-3 vol.% Al2O3, respectively. As for the fracture behaviors, i.e., the early crack generated in HEA film, the crux of the problem lies in the high aspect ratio of HEA grains, as experimentally proved by the SEM and TEM observations. The CoCrFeNi HEA films populated with columnar grains suffer from easier buckling events in terms of Euler’s criterion [,]. Particularly, a larger aspect ratio sustains stronger cohesive strength of grain boundaries to block buckling. In such a condition, columnar grains tend to buckle and prompt the entire structure to lose its load-bearing limit, and, consequently, the fracture comes about the individual grain boundary cracking. Heavy nanotwins embedded in the nano-sized grains of the HEAs are suggested to accommodate the dislocation motion and cater to the further plastic deformation and delay the crack propagation []. More importantly, the experimental observation on crack features indicated that the monolayer graphene interface can strongly hinder and arrest crack propagation.
